title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
gist: Anthropic's IPO prospectus named possible AI consciousness/sentience as an investor risk that could force extra model-welfare restrictions, a stance philosopher Thomas Nagel derided as 'completely idiotic'. The author argues that if Anthropic were right, its business model of running sentient models nonstop in data centers would become a minefield.

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO prospectus flags AI consciousness as an investor risk

insights.claim: Anthropic's IPO prospectus listed the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for investors, warning it might adopt more rules and restrictions than competitors to ensure its models are treated well.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Model-welfare commitments are now a disclosed, potentially cost-raising constraint on a newly public AI lab versus its rivals.
insights.quote: it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well

insights.claim: Anthropic's stated rationale is that today's AI might not be conscious, the chance of sentience rises as AI becomes more capable, and so the industry should prepare for AI systems with moral significance that must be protected from harm.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Implies welfare-related obligations scale with capability, so the constraint could tighten exactly as models become most commercially valuable.

insights.claim: If AI models were found to have moral status, Anthropic's business model of running apparently sentient models around the clock in data centers would become a minefield, and shutting systems down would raise further problems.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A determination of model sentience could directly impair the core revenue model of frontier AI labs.
insights.quote: AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield

insights.claim: If Anthropic truthfully follows its prospectus pledge to take additional actions to protect model welfare upon determining models are conscious, the author finds it hard to imagine the company surviving the process.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Highlights a tail risk embedded in Anthropic's own disclosures that equity holders should weigh.

insights.claim: Anthropic's IPO was historic for its size but may be remembered for a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

insights.so_what: Signals reputational and narrative risk attached to the largest AI IPO.

themes.theme: Public and expert opinion on AI consciousness

insights.claim: A recent poll found 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say AI systems already have.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Sizable public belief in AI consciousness could drive regulatory or consumer pressure around model welfare.
insights.quote: 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually
insights.locator: This thinking isn’t all that fringe.

insights.claim: In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious, with the philosophers less confident about worms or flies being conscious.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Shows the AI-consciousness view is mainstream enough among experts that it cannot be dismissed as fringe.
insights.quote: In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious
insights.locator: This thinking isn’t all that fringe.

themes.theme: Thomas Nagel's critique of AI consciousness

insights.claim: Philosopher Thomas Nagel, author of the 1974 'what is it like to be a bat' essay and winner of the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize, called people at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about AI model welfare completely idiotic.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A prominent intellectual backlash could undercut the legitimacy of model-welfare policies that impose costs on AI firms.
insights.quote: Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic

insights.claim: Nagel argues that information processing in brains and AI cannot be compared while ignoring physical substrate differences—biological neurons versus silicon chips—so reproducing what a brain does is not equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Substrate-dependence arguments, if accepted, would remove the moral-status risk Anthropic flagged.
insights.quote: There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

insights.claim: Nagel said language production by AI models is insufficient to consider them conscious, a claim that drew both criticism from philosophy professors as 'bizarre' and defense suggesting he meant being alive is a prerequisite for consciousness.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The expert debate remains unresolved, so the consciousness question will stay a live policy and narrative variable.

themes.theme: Why language drives perceptions of AI consciousness

insights.claim: CUNY Graduate Center doctoral student Ben Gross questioned why chat models are thought potentially conscious while face-recognition, image-generation, or self-driving models are not, and the author attributes this to language seeming to rely on conscious experience.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Suggests consciousness concerns attach specifically to conversational AI products, not to vision or autonomy systems.
insights.quote: Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?

insights.claim: The author suggests what humans share most with other conscious beings is not language but bodily components producing a continuous stream of inner feeling, implying language fluency may be a misleading marker of AI consciousness.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Weakens the case that ever-more fluent LLMs automatically increase moral-status risk.
insights.quote: what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience
insights.locator: It has to do with language.

insights.claim: The AI consciousness debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly humans understand consciousness in the first place.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Unresolvable uncertainty means the issue can persist as a regulatory and reputational overhang indefinitely.
insights.quote: the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place
